semantic_correction.stem: During a scheduled telehealth follow-up, a client suddenly develops one-sided facial droop, weakness of one arm, and slurred speech. The nurse confirmed the client's exact current address at the start of the visit. What should the nurse do?

options.A: Activate the telehealth emergency plan using the confirmed location so local emergency services can respond immediately.
options.B: Continue the telehealth neurologic assessment before deciding whether the client needs emergency or in-person care.
options.C: End the visit and advise the client to have a family member drive to the nearest clinic for an urgent same-day assessment.
options.D: Ask the client to rest and reconnect after a short interval to determine whether the weakness and speech changes resolve.

semantic_correction.rationale: CDC stroke guidance updated May 19, 2026 identifies sudden facial weakness, arm weakness, and slurred or abnormal speech as stroke warning signs and directs immediate emergency activation rather than private transport. HHS telehealth emergency-planning guidance specifically notes that stroke can arise during a virtual encounter and recommends confirming the patient's exact current location so the appropriate local emergency response can be activated. Because this client develops a classic acute stroke-warning pattern during telehealth and the nurse already confirmed the exact location, the nurse should activate the telehealth emergency plan so local emergency services can respond immediately. Continuing a routine virtual assessment, arranging private transport, or waiting to see whether the symptoms resolve would delay emergency evaluation. The 2026 NCSBN NCLEX-RN Test Plan includes using information-technology resources to promote quality care and prioritizing client care based on acuity. Therefore A is the uniquely best answer.
semantic_correction.educational_objective: During telehealth, recognize new focal neurologic deficits as an emergency and use the client's confirmed location to activate the local emergency-response plan without delaying for further routine virtual assessment.
semantic_correction.source_organization: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), Telehealth.HHS.gov; Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC); National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
semantic_correction.source_document_title: Creating an emergency plan; Signs and Symptoms of Stroke; 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan
semantic_correction.source_version_date: HHS telehealth emergency-plan page last updated August 18, 2023 and rechecked August 19, 2026; CDC Signs and Symptoms of Stroke dated May 19, 2026; NCSBN Test Plan published 2025 and effective April 1, 2026 through March 31, 2029
semantic_correction.source_locator: HHS Telehealth > Creating an emergency plan — emergencies during telehealth may include stroke; confirm the patient's exact current location at the beginning of each appointment; know emergency numbers for that location and establish what will happen during an emergency. CDC Stroke > Signs and Symptoms — sudden one-sided weakness, facial droop and speech difficulty are stroke warning signs; call emergency services immediately and do not use private transport. NCSBN 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan > Management of Care > Information Technology, printed p. 22 / PDF p. 26 — utilize resources including information technology to promote quality client care. Management of Care > Establishing Priorities, printed p. 21 / PDF p. 25 — prioritize delivery of client care based on acuity.

semantic_correction.correction_summary_append: RULE1 cleanup: retired a low-discrimination telehealth-documentation recall item with weak distractors. Rebuilt the UID into a direct telehealth emergency-response decision in which the RN recognizes an acute stroke-warning pattern and uses the already-confirmed client location to activate local emergency response.

audit_findings_append.finding: The replacement tests a concrete entry-level safety action rather than documentation terminology. Current CDC stroke guidance supports immediate emergency activation, and HHS telehealth guidance supports using the patient's confirmed location for local emergency response.
audit_findings_append.source_authority: HHS Telehealth; CDC; NCSBN 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan
audit_findings_append.source_locator: HHS Creating an emergency plan; CDC Signs and Symptoms of Stroke; NCSBN Establishing Priorities printed p. 21 / PDF p. 25 and Information Technology printed p. 22 / PDF p. 26

scope_exclusions.remote_911_routing: The item does not claim that a distant clinician should place a standard 911 call from the clinician's own location. HHS notes that emergency-response planning must account for the patient's location; the answer therefore uses the local telehealth emergency plan and confirmed location.
scope_exclusions.stroke_diagnosis: The nurse is not asked to make a definitive stroke diagnosis. The item tests recognition of a stroke-warning pattern that warrants emergency response.
scope_exclusions.thrombolysis_window: No treatment time window, NIH Stroke Scale threshold, blood-pressure criterion, thrombolytic dose, or thrombectomy eligibility rule is asserted.
scope_exclusions.private_transport: The item follows current CDC guidance that suspected stroke should trigger emergency medical services rather than private transport.

near_duplicate_check.note: Targeted GitHub search for 'telehealth stroke emergency location 911' returned no indexed repository match. No broad bank rescan was performed.

option_audit.A: Correct. It uses the previously confirmed telehealth location to activate the appropriate local emergency response without delaying a stroke-warning presentation.
option_audit.B: Plausible because telehealth allows additional assessment, but the supplied focal neurologic signs already warrant emergency response and further routine assessment should not delay it.
option_audit.C: Plausible because urgent in-person evaluation is required, but CDC advises emergency medical services rather than private transport for suspected stroke.
option_audit.D: Plausible if symptoms were minor or nonspecific, but transient or improving focal stroke symptoms still require urgent medical evaluation rather than observation for resolution.

ambiguity_check: No second defensible best answer. The stem presents three classic new focal stroke-warning signs and supplies the exact telehealth location. B delays emergency action for more virtual assessment, C substitutes private transport, and D waits for symptom resolution. A alone initiates the appropriate emergency response immediately.

cueing_check.note: Exact character counts were calculated from the stored strings. All four alternatives are within seven characters and use parallel telehealth-response actions; the correct answer is not length-cued.
